skill.title: Python
skill.summary: The data model, scope, mutability and concurrency behaviour behind everyday Python.
skill.description: Build an accurate model of what Python does at runtime: object identity, references, default arguments, closures and the trade-offs between threads, processes and asyncio.

questions.title: The surprising default argument
questions.prompt: What does the second `print` call output?
questions.code:
def add_item(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

print(add_item("a"))
print(add_item("b"))
questions.hint: When is the expression `[]` in the signature evaluated: once, or on every call?

options.text: It raises `TypeError` because lists cannot be default values

questions.explanation: Default values are evaluated once, when `def` runs, so every call that omits `bucket` shares the same list object. The second call appends to the list that already contains `'a'`. The idiomatic fix is `bucket=None` and creating a new list inside the function.
rubric: Identifies that default values are evaluated once at function definition time.
Explains that all calls without `bucket` share one mutable list.
Proposes the `None` sentinel pattern as a fix.
misconceptions: Default values are re-created on every call.
Mutable defaults are rejected by the interpreter.
questions.acceptance_criteria: States the second call prints ['a', 'b'] and attributes it to the default list being created once at definition time.

questions.title: Equality versus identity
questions.code:
a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
print(a == b, a is b)
questions.hint: `==` asks whether two values are equal. `is` asks something else.

options.text: `True True`
`True False`
`False False`
`False True`

questions.explanation: `==` compares values using `__eq__`, and the lists hold equal elements. `is` compares identity, and the two literals create two distinct list objects. Use `is` for singletons such as `None`, not for comparing values.
rubric: Distinguishes value equality (`==`) from object identity (`is`).
Recognises that two list literals create two separate objects.
Knows `is` is appropriate for singletons such as `None`.
misconceptions: `is` is a stricter or faster form of `==`.
Equal literals always refer to the same object.

resources.title: Python reference: Objects, values and types

questions.acceptance_criteria: Answers True False and distinguishes value equality from object identity.

questions.title: References, shallow copies and deep copies
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between assigning a reference, making a shallow copy and making a deep copy. Use a nested list as an example and state exactly what each approach lets a later mutation affect.
questions.hint: Consider `a = [[1], [2]]; b = a.copy(); a[0].append(9)`. What does `b` contain now?
questions.explanation: Assignment binds a second name to the same object. A shallow copy creates a new outer container whose elements are the same inner objects, so mutating an inner list is visible through both. A deep copy recursively copies nested mutable objects, so no mutable state is shared. Deep copies cost more and are unnecessary for immutable contents.
rubric: Explains that assignment creates another reference to the same object.
Explains that a shallow copy creates a new outer container but shares the inner objects.
Explains that a deep copy recursively copies nested objects.
Uses a concrete nested example and states the observable difference after mutation.
Mentions the cost trade-off or that immutable contents make deep copies unnecessary.
misconceptions: `list.copy()` or slicing produces a fully independent copy of nested data.
Assignment copies the object.

resources.title: Python library: copy — shallow and deep copy operations

questions.acceptance_criteria: Correctly describes what assignment, a shallow copy and a deep copy each share after a nested mutation.

questions.title: Closures created in a loop
questions.code:
fns = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in fns])
questions.hint: Does each lambda capture the value of `i` or the variable `i`?

options.text: It raises `NameError` because `i` is out of scope

questions.explanation: Closures capture variables, not values, and look them up when called. All three lambdas share the comprehension's single `i`, which is 2 after the last iteration. Bind the current value with a default argument (`lambda i=i: i`) or `functools.partial`.
rubric: States that closures capture variables and resolve them at call time (late binding).
Identifies that the loop variable's final value is 2, not 3.
Offers a fix such as a default argument or `functools.partial`.
misconceptions: Each lambda snapshots `i` when it is created.
The loop variable ends one past the last value produced by `range`.
Comprehension variables are inaccessible to closures defined inside them.

resources.title: Python FAQ: Why do lambdas defined in a loop all return the same result?

questions.acceptance_criteria: Answers [2, 2, 2] and explains late binding of the shared loop variable.

questions.title: Choosing threads, processes or asyncio
questions.prompt: You have two workloads: (1) resizing thousands of images in pure Python, and (2) calling a slow third-party HTTP API ten thousand times. For each, would you use threads, processes or asyncio in standard CPython, and why? Describe what limits each approach.
questions.hint: Separate work that waits on I/O from work that keeps the CPU busy, then consider what the GIL serialises.
questions.explanation: In standard CPython the GIL lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, so threads do not speed up CPU-bound pure-Python work; processes (e.g. `ProcessPoolExecutor`) do, at the cost of serialisation and memory. I/O-bound work spends its time waiting, so threads or asyncio both help; asyncio scales to many concurrent requests cheaply but requires non-blocking libraries throughout. Free-threaded CPython builds (3.13+) change the CPU-bound picture but are opt-in.
rubric: Classifies image resizing as CPU-bound and the API calls as I/O-bound.
Explains that the GIL prevents threads from running Python bytecode in parallel in standard CPython.
Recommends processes for the CPU-bound workload and notes serialisation or memory costs.
Recommends asyncio or threads for I/O-bound work and notes asyncio needs non-blocking libraries.
Mentions bounding concurrency (e.g. a semaphore or pool size) to respect the third-party API.
misconceptions: Threads always make Python code run in parallel.
asyncio speeds up CPU-bound work.
Calling a blocking library from a coroutine is fine because it is inside `async def`.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Matches processes to the CPU-bound workload and asyncio or threads to the I/O-bound one, justified by the GIL.

questions.title: Sequential awaits versus gather
questions.prompt: Each call to `work` sleeps for one second. Roughly how many seconds does this program print?
questions.code:
import asyncio, time

async def work(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    return n

async def main():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    a = await work(1)
    b = await work(2)
    c = await asyncio.gather(work(3), work(4))
    print(round(time.perf_counter() - start))

asyncio.run(main())
questions.hint: Which awaits wait for the previous one to finish, and which overlap?
questions.explanation: Awaiting a coroutine runs it to completion before the next line starts, so the first two awaits take about one second each. `asyncio.gather` schedules both coroutines on the event loop at once, so their sleeps overlap and the pair takes about one second. The total is about three seconds.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “3”. Awaiting a coroutine runs it to completion before the next line starts, so the first two awaits take about one second each.
rubric: States that consecutive awaits run one after another.
States that `gather` runs the coroutines concurrently.
Adds the durations correctly (1 + 1 + 1).
misconceptions: `async def` functions automatically run in parallel.
`gather` runs coroutines in separate threads.

questions.title: Defining __eq__ without __hash__
questions.prompt: What happens when this program runs?
questions.hint: What must be true of the hashes of two objects that compare equal?

options.text: It prints `1`, because the two points compare equal
It prints `2`, because each instance keeps its default identity hash
It raises `TypeError`, because `Point` instances are unhashable
It raises `AttributeError`, because `__hash__` is not defined

questions.explanation: A class that defines `__eq__` without defining `__hash__` has its `__hash__` set to `None`, because objects that compare equal must have equal hashes and the default identity hash would break that rule. Instances therefore cannot go into a set or be dict keys, and building the set raises `TypeError`. Define `__hash__` from the same fields as `__eq__`, ideally on an immutable class such as a frozen dataclass.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “It raises `TypeError`, because `Point` instances are unhashable”. A class that defines `__eq__` without defining `__hash__` has its `__hash__` set to `None`, because objects that compare equal must have equal hashes and the default identity hash would break that rule.
rubric: Explains that defining `__eq__` sets `__hash__` to None.
Connects it to the rule that equal objects must have equal hashes.
Proposes a consistent `__hash__` or a frozen dataclass.
misconceptions: Objects keep the default identity hash after overriding `__eq__`.
Any object can be put in a set.

questions.title: Is the GIL a lock for your code?
questions.prompt: Four threads each run `increment()` once on standard (GIL) CPython. Is the final value of `counter` guaranteed to be 400000?
questions.hint: How many separate steps does `counter += 1` involve, and can a thread switch happen between them?

options.text: Yes: the GIL makes every Python statement atomic
Yes: integers are immutable, so updates cannot interfere
No: it is always lower, because threads overwrite each other
No: `+=` is a read-modify-write; protect it with a `Lock`

questions.explanation: The GIL lets only one thread execute bytecode at a time, but a thread can be switched out between the load, add and store steps of `counter += 1`. An update can then be lost. Whether that happens on a given run depends on the interpreter version and timing, so the program may print 400000 many times and still be wrong. Use a `threading.Lock` around the update, or avoid shared mutable state. Free-threaded builds make races more likely, not less.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “No: `+=` is a read-modify-write; protect it with a `Lock”. The GIL lets only one thread execute bytecode at a time, but a thread can be switched out between the load, add and store steps of `counter += 1`.
rubric: States that the result is not guaranteed.
Explains that `+=` is several bytecode steps that can interleave.
Explains that the GIL does not make compound operations atomic.
Proposes a lock or a design without shared mutable state.
misconceptions: The GIL makes Python code thread-safe.
A race always produces a wrong result on every run.

questions.title: Sorting a list in place
questions.hint: What does a mutating list method return?

options.text: `None`
It raises `TypeError`

questions.explanation: `list.sort()` sorts the list in place and returns `None`, a Python convention for methods that mutate. Assigning its result rebinds `nums` to `None`. Use `nums.sort()` on its own line, or `sorted(nums)`, which returns a new sorted list.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “None”. `list.sort()` sorts the list in place and returns `None`, a Python convention for methods that mutate.
rubric: States that `list.sort()` returns None.
Explains that it mutates the list in place.
Contrasts it with `sorted()`.
misconceptions: `list.sort()` returns the sorted list.
Methods always return their object.

questions.title: Summing the same generator twice
questions.code:
squares = (x * x for x in range(3))
print(sum(squares), sum(squares))
questions.hint: Can a generator be rewound after it has produced its values?

options.text: It raises `StopIteration`

questions.explanation: A generator expression produces its values once. The first `sum` consumes 0 + 1 + 4 = 5; the second finds the generator exhausted and sums nothing, giving 0. No exception escapes, because `sum` stops cleanly when iteration ends. Use a list if you need to iterate more than once.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “5 0”. A generator expression produces its values once.
rubric: Explains that a generator can be iterated only once.
Computes the first sum as 5.
Explains that the exhausted generator sums to 0 without an error.
misconceptions: Generators restart each time you iterate them.
Iterating an exhausted generator raises an error.

questions.title: Threads that do not speed up a CPU-bound job
questions.prompt: On standard (GIL) CPython, a function hashes passwords in pure Python and takes 8 seconds for a batch on one core. Running the batch across 4 threads in a `ThreadPoolExecutor` still takes about 8 seconds on a 4-core machine. What is the best explanation and fix?
questions.hint: Is the work waiting on I/O or executing Python code?

options.text: The pool defaults to one worker; pass `max_workers=4`
Only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time; use `ProcessPoolExecutor`
Threads must be started with `asyncio.run` to use more than one core
Context switching overhead cancels the gain; use 16 threads instead

questions.explanation: The GIL lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, so CPU-bound pure-Python work does not run in parallel across threads. Threads help when the work waits on I/O or calls C code that releases the GIL (such as `hashlib` on large inputs). For CPU-bound Python, use processes (`ProcessPoolExecutor`), which each have their own interpreter, at the cost of pickling arguments and results. Free-threaded builds (3.13+) change this but are not the default.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “Only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time; use `ProcessPoolExecutor”. The GIL lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, so CPU-bound pure-Python work does not run in parallel across threads.
rubric: Explains the GIL limits bytecode to one thread at a time.
Distinguishes CPU-bound from I/O-bound work.
Proposes processes, noting their overhead.
Mentions free-threaded builds or GIL-releasing C code as nuance.
misconceptions: Threads always use multiple cores in Python.
More threads always finish CPU work faster.
